## Design

### 2026-11-03: In this session I did the ALU, and registers. First I did the ALU, it wasn't too complicated, I only had to chain two 4 bit adders together, and wire all the inputs and outputs correctly.

**2h**

In this session I did the ALU, and registers. First I did the ALU, it wasn't too complicated, I only had to chain two 4 bit adders together, and wire all the inputs and outputs correctly.

![Screenshot from 2026-11-02 16-13-09](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/1cbaf337dde008fa000c5e05593c2377a68872c1927b5d40f69a7d2585e285da.png)

Regarding the inputs and outputs, I did the registers and the BUS. For the registers I did registers for 2 numbers, the ones to add. For each one, they are done by wiring up two 4 bit registers together, and adding clock, and save signals, etc. One harder part was finding out how buses work, since KiCad does it pretty weird, but I managed to figure it out.

![Screenshot from 2026-11-02 17-07-58](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/3c0d8f0eeb89e73396378f286bcf58ca1ec463c12cea1c9f47b70ed3db09681c.png)

After the registers, I also did some buffers for the ALU, so it can be controlled when it writes to the BUS, so here is how that turned out in the end.

![Screenshot from 2026-11-02 18-27-10](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/8ad8bf5ddcfa4dc57ec86f4a50a2f0dc77748a7631f7f75df18e628d97a38442.png)

That's it for today, my next plan is to do the clock and the program counter tomorrow, so I might research a bit about that tonight.

### 2026-11-03: So in this session I did the  clock and the  program counter. First for the clock, I did the schematic mainly based on Ben Eaters design, he explains stuff really well, and for the clock my design mat

**2h**

So in this session I did the  clock and the  program counter. First for the clock, I did the schematic mainly based on Ben Eaters design, he explains stuff really well, and for the clock my design matched his, so I could follow his explanations. I built a clock with 2 modes, a regular timed, and also a manual button clock based design. Here is the astable(regular) timer design:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/8eae9bfe27b196f71ea3f73c1f9e11c5f9a89231902319b92be5d4910feee7a3.png)

And also here is the monostable(button controlled) design:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/d01c203715de0897e71fb31a447f0852e552d8bac9b56516dc16626c90b1d2bc.png)
(for the debouncing I used a 555 timer)

I then built a combined bistable design, that means that there is a switch that lets me select between the 2 modes, with it's own debouncing:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/83c2f30f71ac28560d0b77abf08c3122abca2d4bed31a3f05aa3e09e7b5d4a76.png)

Then I had to combine the 3 outputs, to make the select signal actually select between the 2, and I also added a halt signal that stops the clock when pulled high, and here is how that turned out:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/e2c1e726cdbb9663f1317c48891d76a7affd70d765c5d4fb7336af49be2fe861.png)

After that I built the program counter, which was a much simpler process, mainly just wiring stuff up to the bus, and a few control signals:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/62f56ed8e0bdbaecba7105ace0bfba3ead6e58068010a3ba698eb9d5aa777d4f.png)

### 2026-11-04: Soo in this session I did the PROM. I decided to go with a harvard architecture, that just means that I have a seperate PROM(program read only memory), which stores the program, and a DRAM(data random

**2h**

Soo in this session I did the PROM. I decided to go with a harvard architecture, that just means that I have a seperate PROM(program read only memory), which stores the program, and a DRAM(data random access memory), for storing stuff like data and variables. I went with a 12 bit construction, because if I would have stayed with the regular 8 bit design, it would only have 4 opcodes, and that would need an EEPROM for controlling everything, and that would be more complicated and costly. Like this I have 4 pins for an address, and 8 opcodes, for different operations. For the RAM module I found no symbol, so I had to do a custom one, it doesn't look the best, but its usable:

![Screenshot from 2026-11-04 17-08-11](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/c8c4e8a76ab3a0ef12e4da07e4568844cd180857de4b9baf2f1efe7d484da49e.png)

After that I just had to chain 3 of these together, and connect inverters, because the outputs are inverted, and I also hooked up some dip switches, so that it could be programmed, and had to connect everything. The wiring didn't end up too beautiful, but it is functional:

![Screenshot from 2026-11-04 18-48-13](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/08274ed3f411729c98bfa0cb936b3cf97852efab778a5e59ce680ba01d9471f1.png)

I know I'm still missing the instruction register, and I'm also not sure, how I'll do the control logic, so I'll need to think it through, but overall I think I'm doing pretty good.

### 2026-11-05: In this session, I did the DRAM. I thought it would be an easy thing, but as it turned out, it wasn't too simple, First I did a MAR(Memory Address Register), which was a bit complicated, most of the h

**2h**

In this session, I did the DRAM. I thought it would be an easy thing, but as it turned out, it wasn't too simple, First I did a MAR(Memory Address Register), which was a bit complicated, most of the harder stuff was just to wire it up in a way, so that I can use a push switch, and dip switches to manually save an address into the register, but in the end I figured it out using a multiplexer and 2 AND gates.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/1aaf4bf1ad029b7bd875361a3eb7e84448c641793280fee052fd1ee6ec24f7da.png)

After that I started working on the RAM modules themselves. They weren't too hard to wire, I did them similarly to my PROM, only harder part was again having to use 2 multiplexers to be able to select between reading from the bus, and using dip switches to enter values manually

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/1ef455a160cb2587d6ab3a88b63dd6d15b8e4009158399230ffecbeffad39aa8.png)

(I don't really like how the wiring turned out, but if I have time later, I'll try making it cleaner)
After that, I just had to make it output onto the BUS. That wasn't too complicated, just a simple bus driver module. I made it controllable by 2 signals, one for reading from the BUS, and saving it to an address, the the other is to read from an address, and save to the BUS. This way I can control it with not too many pins. I also did a plan for the programming, but I did that in a notebook, so I can't include that here. Here is the full finished schematic:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/032c5257ab40db5eb5ab8353aabe2c435db541a779dc6e606c26fd03865eff86.png)

### 2026-11-05: In this session, I did the IR(Instruction Register). For it I just had to connect the DROM outputs to three 4 bit registers, and make the output control stuff. For me this is also the control unit, si

**1.5h**

In this session, I did the IR(Instruction Register). For it I just had to connect the DROM outputs to three 4 bit registers, and make the output control stuff. For me this is also the control unit, since I have no EEPROM running some control logic, instead I built a custom mode to program this. This doesn't follow any standard, I just built it in a way that is relatively easy for me to understand, and is also functional. Since I use a 12 bit PROM, each operation is 12 bits, the first 4 being the address, the code either uses it to access a DRAM address, or have an address to jump to. The last 8 bits are for controlling what writes to, and reads from the bus, and other functionalities, like clock halt, etc. For example 000101001000 saves the sum of the values in reg A and B, and saves them to the 0001 DRAM address. I'll explain it better in the README. Here is the finished schematic:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/0fad8d7608a30fc394c714ddcf9fd5b3c545facbddb51c71a81c74a20123d50e.png)

 After this was done, I had to connect every control pin to what they control, I did that on the main sheet, here is how that turned out. I also changed some global labels to hierarchical labels to make it cleaner, and also I replaced the bus output terminals with another chip, since the one I used was 4 bit, so I needed 2, and now it's 8 bit, so I only need one, and it's also easier to control

![Screenshot from 2026-11-05 21-33-52](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/sDE0sWuzf8SaPJwrIDtc043sSoi90nZ7/c5090aa09db3e592389fe655aa199172b872c3fc60be78879902853bce39c6b7.png)

**1.5h**

In this session, I first did some checking,and after that, I made most of the BOM. For the first part I just ran ERC, I had  a few errors, but most of them could be ignored, but there were some unconnected items that I needed to fix, but after it was finished.

After that I did the BOM. It was honestly pretty straightforward, I just had to find all the parts I needed on LCSC, and add them to the BOM. The hardest part to find was the RAM, they didn't have it on LCSC, so I had to find it on Aliexpress, but after I did that, it was pretty easy. I didn't yet add any passives, and breadboards, wires, etc. only the chips. Here is my original parts list I wrote together:
